walkthroughs.body_html:
Area of Study 1: My Music (Performance) — a core area of GCSE Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area of Study 1: My Music (Performance) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area of Study 1: My Music (Performance).

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What makes a good choice of performance piece?
options: One that suits your level and shows your strengths
The hardest piece you can find
Whatever your friend is playing
A piece you have never practised
Keeping going with a steady pulse
Playing everything very fast
Pausing after each phrase
Improvising new notes

mcqs.q: What is the best way to improve a difficult bar?
options: Isolate it, slow it down and repeat it correctly
Play the whole piece faster
Skip it every time
Only practise the easy sections

mcqs.q: Why is recording your own practice useful?
options: You hear yourself objectively and can target improvements
It replaces the need to practise
It makes the piece shorter
It tunes the instrument automatically

mcqs.q: Does repeating a piece over and over guarantee improvement?
options: No - improvement comes from correct, focused repetition: isolating problems, slowing down and fixing errors before speeding up.
Expression is only required in vocal performances.
Practice makes perfect, so any repetition automatically helps.
You improve most by buying a more expensive instrument.

mcqs.q: Will choosing a harder piece always earn a higher mark?
options: Marks depend mainly on the length of the piece's title.
Difficulty alone impresses, so always pick the hardest piece.
You improve most by buying a more expensive instrument.
No - an accurate, musical performance of a suitable piece scores better than a struggling attempt at one beyond your technique.

mcqs.q: Can dynamics and expression be added at the last minute?
options: Learn the notes first; expression can be sprinkled on the night before.
Expression is only required in vocal performances.
You improve most by buying a more expensive instrument.
It is far better to build them in from early practice so they become part of how you know the piece.

sequence.def: First match repertoire to your strengths and the time requirement
Isolate and slow down difficulties before running the piece
Add dynamics, articulation and phrasing once notes are fluent
Complete run-throughs with accompanist/backing before recording
Perform the programme in one sitting for assessment
Last: send recording and documentation to the exam board
